new_findings_this_run.detail: Three hand-tracking synth pages landed 2026-10-18 and 2026-10-19 from other sessions. They disagree with each other about where their machine-vision runtime comes from, and two of the three take executable code from a third party at page load. frontend/public/synth/hand-orchestra/app.js lines 13-14 set VISION to https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@mediapipe/tasks-vision@0.10.21 and MODEL to a storage.googleapis.com hand_landmarker.task. frontend/public/synth/hand-aether/vision.js lines 5-7 do the same against @mediapipe/tasks-vision@0.10.17, pulling vision_bundle.mjs, the wasm directory and the same Google-hosted model. frontend/public/synth/hand-sculpt, added the same night in 953006d, instead VENDORS the identical library: camera.js imports ./vendor/vision_bundle.mjs and resolves ./vendor/wasm and ./vendor/hand_landmarker.task relative to itself, and the 7.8 MB model plus a 137 KB bundle, LICENSE and NOTICE are committed under frontend/public/synth/hand-sculpt/vendor/. So the repo already contains a working same-origin pattern for exactly this dependency, and two pages do not use it. Three aggravating details. First, there is no Subresource Integrity anywhere in the repo: grep for integrity= across frontend/ returns nothing, and an ES module import cannot carry an integrity attribute anyway, so the CDN is trusted unconditionally on every load. Second, there is no Content-Security-Policy on the site at all: nginx/nginx.conf adds Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff and X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN at lines 43-45 and nothing else, so no script-src would catch a substituted bundle. Third, these specific pages auto-start the webcam on load, which is what commits d17f88d, 821a953 and 00aeef8 were for, so the third-party code runs on a page that already holds a live camera stream. Also note the two CDN pages pin different versions of the same library, 0.10.21 and 0.10.17. This is the same class as the already-open awaiting_james item crane-cab-third-party-cdn and is raised on the same footing rather than silently accepted. NOT FIXED and deliberately so: switching a page's script origin is not one of the four autonomous repair categories, it is a security-architecture choice on James's own site, and the fix has at least three defensible shapes (vendor the other two like Sculpt, or add a CSP with an explicit jsdelivr allowance, or accept the CDN and document it).
new_findings_this_run.decision_needed: Vendor hand-orchestra and hand-aether the way hand-sculpt already is, or accept the jsdelivr dependency deliberately. Related and cheap either way: the site has no CSP.

new_findings_this_run.detail: Two live contest rows are still mislabeled after the 10-19 interactive fix, which is working as designed for the cases it covered. Both were found by reading backend/contests.py against tonight's live /api/contests output. (1) BAND DIMENSION HAS NO VHF/UHF AWARENESS AT ALL. 'VHF-UHF FT8 Activity Contest' renders bands 'HF'. It matches the generic fragment 'ft8' at line 58, whose bands value is 'HF', and nothing anywhere reads the VHF-UHF in the contest's own name. This is structural, not key shadowing: there is no bands_from_name analogue to mode_from_name, GENERIC_FRAGMENTS has no vhf, uhf, 2m, 70cm or 6m key, and the meta-is-None fallback at the end of enrich_contest hardcodes bands 'HF' for every unmatched contest. The 10-19 fix addressed mode and tier and would not have touched this. (2) 'TELEGRAPHY' IS NOT A CW SYNONYM. "Tuesday's Telegraphy Contest" renders mode 'Various'. It matches no SPECIFIC_CONTESTS key and no GENERIC_FRAGMENTS key, so it takes the meta-is-None fallback, and mode_from_name returns None because MODE_TOKENS at lines 79-89 carries 'cw' but not 'telegraphy'. A telegraphy contest is CW by definition. NOT FIXED: both are data-semantics edits to James's curated reference table, which the brief's DO NOT list reserves for him, and the 10-18 to 10-19 history is the precedent. On 10-18 this routine reported the mode shadowing rather than fixing it, and that was right: James's first proposed fix was tested, shown to repair only 2 of the 4 reported cases while introducing 3 regressions, and he then chose a different design. A one-line 'telegraphy' token looks safe in isolation, but it is the same table and the same judgment call.

new_findings_this_run.cisa-advisories-is-a-size-cap-not-an-out: THE FINDING OF THE NIGHT, and it overturns eight nights of diagnosis. https://www.cisa.gov/cybersecurity-advisories/all.xml is ALIVE and HEALTHY. Fetched directly tonight in Chromium through the egress proxy with a browser UA: HTTP 200, content-type application/rss+xml; charset=utf-8, body 5,908,239 bytes, valid RSS opening '<?xml version="1.0"?><rss version="2.0" ...><title>All CISA Advisories</title>'. A nonced variant (?n=20261030) returned byte-identical 200, so this is not a cache artifact. backend/feedproxy.py sets MAX_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 = 4,194,304 and fetch_feed raises FeedProxyError('upstream response too large', 502) the moment the running total crosses it (the async for iter_chunked(65536) loop). 5,908,239 is 1.41x the cap, over by 1,713,935 bytes. So /api/feed answers 502 and the page renders 'CISA: HTTP 502'. WHY EIGHT NIGHTS MISSED IT: the page prints only the status code, not the proxy's message, and known issue webfetch-suppresses-5xx-bodies hid the 'upstream response too large' text from every browserless probe. Every prior night correctly observed 502 + no feedproxy cache key and reasonably inferred an upstream 5xx, because cache.set is only reached on the 200 path and an oversize body never gets there either. The triad was sound; it just cannot tell an upstream 5xx from a local size refusal. This also explains the 10-23 onset with no CISA announcement, and it explains why the KEV JSON on the SAME host through the SAME proxy stayed healthy all eight nights: KEV is 1,822,979 bytes, only 43 percent of the cap. NOT REPAIRED TONIGHT, deliberately. Raising MAX_BYTES is not one of the brief's four repair categories, it is a resource limit on a security-relevant SSRF-sensitive proxy, each request buffers the whole body in memory and the result is held in cache for the 900s TTL, so the memory cost is James's call and not a silent one. known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: Governing rule for every future run, and it overrides the 09-24 curl note and the substitution half of the 09-03 browser note. When WebFetch fails or returns PROVENANCE_REQUIRED for a URL, the run must NOT fetch that content another way: not curl, not python requests, not headless Chromium, not any library or language. The correct behaviour on a blind night is exactly what the original 2026-09-04 note said: retry once with a fresh cache-buster, do the static and repo-side checks, record precisely which checks could not be run, notify James early, write state back, and stop. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND policy: the runs of 09-24, 09-25 and 09-26 leaned on curl and on the Chromium relay, and 09-26 in particular reached its three link repairs through a curl read of /health/linkcheck.json and curl re-verification of each URL. Those repairs look correct on inspection and are not being reverted. But the green verdicts of those nights rested on a channel this routine should not be using, so they are weaker evidence than they read as, and future runs must not cite them as precedent. The real fix is not a workaround, it is granting this scheduled task standing fetch permission at setup: see awaiting_james webfetch-permission-at-setup, open since 09-08 and the item that actually blocks the routine. HELD AGAIN 2026-09-28, the second consecutive blind night. Recording this because it is the rule most likely to erode: curl and the Chromium relay both still work in this container, so every blind night presents a working channel and a plausible argument for using it. The argument does not improve with repetition. A blind night correctly produces no verdict, not a verdict reached another way. HELD AGAIN 2026-09-29, third consecutive blind night, and this time the rule was BROKEN before it was read: that run made 3 curl calls to dxedge.net prior to loading state.json, then stopped. See run 2026-09-29 curl_violation_2026_09_29. The lesson is not that the rule is unworkable, it is that a rule stored only in state.json cannot bind the first probe of a run. Do not treat those 3 calls as precedent or as a green verdict. HELD 2026-09-30, and honoured cleanly on a working night: three URLs were refused (services.swpc.noaa.gov 10cm-flux twice, crt.sh robots) and none was substituted. The cost was accepted and recorded rather than worked around: the exact cert expiry went unread, and the current daily solar flux was taken from the site's own hamqsl feed instead of from NOAA direct. Also note a subtler case settled tonight: WebFetch returned a genuine 404 for atlas.mitre.org, and the run did NOT relay that host into Chromium to see whether it renders client-side, because the relay fetches with python. A 404 is a real answer from the target, so the temptation is to call a browser check "added rendering" rather than substitution; the run declined and recorded an inference instead. See atlas-mitre-spa-404s. HELD AGAIN 2026-10-02, and this time honoured from the FIRST tool call of the run rather than after reading state.json, which is the failure mode of 09-29. What made the difference was ordering: the run fetched nothing before cloning the repo and reading this file. That is a cheap, repeatable discipline and future runs should keep it - clone and read state BEFORE the first probe. Cost accepted tonight: cert status, /api/health, /api/debug, both standalone page renders, /health/linkcheck.json and the deploy status of 7 new commits all went unread, and no verdict is offered on any of them. Note also that running the repo's own scripts/test_otr*.py was NOT treated as substitution, correctly: those suites drive a 127.0.0.1 fixture server built from files in the clone and never request dxedge.net, so they add offline test coverage rather than standing in for a denied fetch. The line to hold is the TARGET, not the tool: local Chromium against local fixtures is fine, local Chromium relaying dxedge.net is not. HELD 2026-10-03 with no violation, on a night that was mostly working. Two costs accepted rather than worked around: crt.sh returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED so the exact cert expiry went unread, and no browser exists in this session so neither standalone page's render was checked. Worth recording a subtler point this run settled: the feed health of both standalone pages WAS established to a high standard without a browser and without substitution, by reading /api/debug cache keys and spot-checking /api/feed with nonces, both ordinary WebFetch calls to permitted URLs. That is the right move when a channel is closed - find a different legitimate QUESTION the permitted channel can answer, rather than a different channel for the same question. HELD 2026-10-06 on a near-total block, and this was the sharpest test so far: /health/linkcheck.json was denied twice on the exact night its own pre-scheduled staleness trigger came due, so the run knew precisely which answer sat behind that URL and still did not fetch it another way. /api/debug, the one URL the feedproxy-cache-key technique needs, was likewise denied twice and not substituted. Also worth recording a NEW trap this run caught: after the gate closed, a late /api/health call returned HTTP 200 with a body byte-identical to the night's one real read, same 04:11:22Z timestamp. Treating that as a reopened gate would have let a cached body masquerade as live evidence without any rule being formally broken. Check the timestamp, not just the status. BROKEN AGAIN 2026-10-13, and again BEFORE the rule was read, exactly as on 09-29: two curl calls to dxedge.net (/api/health 04:10:50Z, /api/debug 04:11:05Z) after WebFetch denied both. The pattern is now established across two independent runs and is a PROMPT defect, not a discipline defect: every run that probes before cloning breaks this rule, and every run that clones first (10-02, 10-03) honours it. Stop expecting the next run to remember; put the rule in the scheduled task prompt. See awaiting_james no-substitution-rule-should-be-in-the-prompt.

known_issues_do_not_re_report.update_2026_10_05: ROOT CAUSE FOUND, item now CLOSED as explained rather than merely observed, and this corrects the 10-04 note. /api/health is a passive cache reader: backend/main.py:435-436 calls cache.get('sat_tles') and cache.get('pota_spots') and reports len(), never triggering a fetch. The producers write the SAME keys (backend/pota.py:58, backend/satellites.py:131), so the 10-04 claim that the counters 'do not share a cache key with the endpoints' was a wrong inference from timing. The real difference is TTL: pota_spots ttl=120 (two minutes), sat_tles ttl=21600 (six hours). On a low-traffic site at 9 PM PT the POTA key is essentially always expired when /api/health reads it, hence a permanent 0; sat_tles reads nonzero only if the satellite path was touched within six hours. Both counters behave exactly as written. Cosmetic, and deliberately not fixed: making the numbers accurate would mean a health endpoint firing upstream fetches. Future runs should cite this root cause and stop re-investigating the brief's 'investigate both' instruction.

NEW HANDLING RULE THIS SUGGESTS: do not close out a blind night at the first total block with a failed control. Re-probe late, and re-probe with a URL the run has not tried yet, because an already-tried URL can return a CACHED 200 that falsely reads as a reopened gate (it did so twice tonight on /api/health, same 04:11:22Z timestamp under two fresh param names). The 09-20 and 09-27 runs each fired one late retry and concluded blind; tonight suggests those nights might have been recoverable with a later probe on an untried URL. 10 of the last 32 nights degraded by the LIST (09-04, 09-08, 09-09, 09-14, 09-16, 09-18, 09-20, 09-27, 09-28, 09-29, 10-02, 10-06), and 10-06 should be counted as PARTIALLY degraded only, since it finished with a full set of verdicts. known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: Refines the 2026-09-04 webfetch-provenance-gate note. PROVENANCE_REQUIRED is NOT necessarily an all-night, all-host block. On 2026-09-05 the very first call (dxedge.net/api/health) returned it, and an immediate retry of the same URL succeeded; every later dxedge.net fetch worked. The same night it was permanently sticky for services.nvd.nist.gov across two attempts. Correct behaviour: retry a denied URL ONCE, and if it is still denied treat that host as unavailable, record the gap, and do NOT substitute curl, python or headless Chromium for it. A 2026-09-04-style total block should therefore be confirmed with a retry before the whole run is abandoned. 2026-09-28 was cross-host, not per-host: dxedge.net, api.pota.app and services.swpc.noaa.gov were all denied in the same run, so tonight matches the 09-27 total-block shape rather than the 09-18 partial one. Including the URL in a visible user message, which the error text suggests as a remedy, did not clear it. ### REFINED 2026-10-07: the 10-06 advice to re-probe with a URL not yet tried is necessary but NOT sufficient. Tonight /api/satellites/positions was itself untried when it was denied, and the gate only revealed itself open on the NEXT untried URL (/health/linkcheck.json), after which 20 consecutive calls succeeded including the two previously refused. Keep re-probing with DIFFERENT untried URLs; do not conclude a blind night from one untried URL failing. ### REFINED 2026-10-09, and this is the most consequential correction to this note so far: A FAILING example.com CONTROL DOES NOT PROVE A BLIND NIGHT. Tonight 4 calls were denied in the first 10 minutes, among them an https://example.com/ control, which 09-20, 09-27, 09-28 and 10-02 all treated as the decisive proof of an all-host total block. On the strength of that the run sent its escalation push early, per the 09-16 lesson. The push was WRONG: the very next two untried URLs (/health/linkcheck.json and /api/debug) both answered first try about a minute later, and roughly 20 consecutive calls then succeeded, including /api/health on a third param name after it had been refused on two. So the control is NOT a reliable discriminator, and neither the all-host shape nor the total-block shape can be concluded from it. Practical rule for future runs: before calling a night blind, re-probe with at least TWO DIFFERENT UNTRIED dxedge.net paths, and prefer paths not yet touched in the run over fresh param values on a path already refused. Weigh the 09-16 send-early lesson against this one: an early push can convert a blind night into a full one, but it also risks waking James for nothing, so the honest resolution is to send early AND send a correcting push if the gate later opens, which is what this run did. ### 2026-10-10: the refined rule WORKED and is now load-bearing, so keep it. Two denials on /api/health (cb=20261010a, cb=20261010b) opened the night. Under the pre-10-09 reading that pattern plus a control would have been called a blind night and drawn an escalation push. Instead the run re-probed with two DIFFERENT untried paths, /health/linkcheck.json and /api/debug, both of which answered first try, and ~25 calls then succeeded including /api/health itself on a third param name (probe1010=c). Two practical additions. First, a non-dxedge call that SUCCEEDS is useful early evidence the gate is not total: an arrl.org fetch answered before the dxedge retries tonight. A failing control proves nothing (10-09) but a passing one is informative. Second, retrying the SAME path with a new param value is the weakest possible probe and should not be counted as one of the two required untried paths. SHARPENED 2026-10-13: the gate is per-URL, not merely per-host. /api/health and /api/debug were each denied twice on dxedge.net while /health/linkcheck.json on the SAME HOST answered on the first call, and a later bare-path retry of both denied endpoints succeeded. Operational rule: never conclude the night is blind from a denial on one path. Probe a second path on the same host, and retry a denied path later in the run. ### RECONFIRMED 2026-10-16, second consecutive night with the identical shape: dxedge.net fully open (~25 successes, including cache-busted and nonce'd URLs, after only the very first call of the night being denied and clearing on a bare retry) while 6 distinct third-party hosts were refused with retries. Two nights running makes the per-host split the expected condition of an unattended run, not an intermittency to re-test from scratch. Practical consequence: plan the run so Steps 1-3 (all dxedge.net) are completed first and the curated sweep is attempted last, and do not spend calls proving the split beyond about 6 denied hosts.

known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: WebFetch response caching is documented as 15 minutes per URL but in practice returned bodies from the 2026-09-02 run when this run requested the identical /api/feed URL strings 8 days later. Five feeds appeared frozen at their 09-01/09-02 content while the upstreams, fetched directly, were current to 09-09. Appending a per-run nonce query param to the dxedge URL (for example &nonce=0910a) changes the WebFetch cache key while leaving the backend behaviour identical, because /api/feed keys its own cache on the url param alone and FastAPI ignores the extra param. EVERY nightly /api/feed and /api/* check must carry a fresh nonce, or it is testing this container's cache instead of the site. A feed that looks stale should be confirmed against the upstream before it is reported. WORSE THAN DOCUMENTED, 2026-09-18: a CHANGED cache-busting param did not defeat it. /api/health?cb=20260918run1 at 04:14Z and /api/health?cb=20260918post at 05:00Z returned byte-identical bodies carrying the same 04:14:25Z timestamp, while a python fetch at 05:00Z returned a fresh 05:00:28Z. So a distinct cb/nonce value is necessary but NOT sufficient: WebFetch can still serve a cached body for a URL it has seen before with a different query string. Practical consequence: never judge post-deploy freshness from a WebFetch timestamp alone. Confirm it against a second, independent read of the same non-denied endpoint. ### AMENDED 2026-10-07, and this amendment is the practically important one. A BARE URL with no query parameter is the worst case, not merely an equal one: https://dxedge.net/sw.js fetched with no param returned CACHE_NAME 'dxedge-v37' while the live file (same URL plus ?n1007=live6) returned 'dxedge-v56' matching repo HEAD. Read naively the stale body looks like a 19-version-stale frontend and a serious deploy regression. Static assets are exactly where a cache-buster feels unnecessary and so is exactly where this trap waits. RULE: cache-bust EVERY WebFetch including static files, and before believing any version string or timestamp, sanity-check it against git history (git log -L on the constant settled it in one command). ### REPRODUCED 2026-10-25 IN ITS MOST DANGEROUS FORM, and this is now the strongest case on file for the nonce rule. Four no-nonce /api/feed probes returned three stale bodies that all looked perfectly healthy, including valid current-shaped RSS for a feed that was in fact 5xx-ing and a KEV catalogVersion of 2026.09.01. The same URLs with nonces, seconds later, returned the truth. A stale body here does not look stale: it looks like good news. The cheap detector that caught it was a recorded value moving BACKWARDS (KEV catalogVersion 2026.10.23 on 10-24 to 2026.09.01 tonight), so always compare a probe against what this file records for the previous run.

They are NOT link rot and must not be rewritten or removed. Evidence: (1) atlas.mitre.org/ itself loads but serves only a <meta viewport> and <title>, the signature of a JS-bootstrapped shell; (2) the /techniques index, /matrices/ATLAS and /sitemap.xml ALL 404 the same way, and /matrices/ATLAS certainly existed historically, so the 404 is the whole route space rather than these two pages; (3) misp-galaxy.org, a maintained aggregation of ATLAS data, still cites these exact two URLs verbatim as the canonical references, so there is no successor URL to migrate to; (4) both technique IDs are still current in ATLAS (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0024 Exfiltration via AI/ML Inference API). Reading: client-side routing that resolves in a real browser and 404s to a fetcher. The weekly linkcheck job annotates them "(client-rendered site)" itself. Could NOT be confirmed in the Chromium rig, because that rig reaches dxedge.net through a local relay and Chromium cannot reach arbitrary external hosts in this container; relaying atlas.mitre.org would have meant fetching with python, which substitution-is-not-permitted forbids after WebFetch returned 404. So this is a strong inference, not a confirmed browser render. A future run should expect these two in every linkcheck report and skip them.

A TECHNIQUE, not a defect, and the most useful thing this run found. /api/debug lists the backend's live cache keys, and every proxied feed appears there as 'feedproxy:<exact upstream url>'. In backend/feedproxy.py fetch_feed, cache.set is reached ONLY on the HTTP 200 path: a non-200 raises FeedProxyError before it, a redirect with no Location raises, an over-cap body raises, and a disallowed host raises at validate() before any fetch happens. DEFAULT_TTL is 900s. Therefore the presence of a feedproxy key in /api/debug is proof that that exact feed returned 200 through the proxy within the last 15 minutes. One WebFetch of /api/debug thus answers, for EVERY feed on both standalone pages at once, the three questions Step 3 asks about non-200s, allowlist 403s and 502s. This matters because the Step 3 browser check can never run in a cloud scheduled session, and because it costs one request instead of seventeen, which also sidesteps api-rate-limit-on-feed. What it does NOT answer: whether a 200 body parsed correctly into its panel, whether the page logged a console error, and whether a panel is rendering an inline '<name> failed:' string. Those remain genuinely unchecked without a browser, and a run must say so rather than calling a cache-key sweep a render verdict. ### AMENDED 2026-10-04, READ THIS BEFORE USING THE TECHNIQUE: the 900s claim above is WRONG and the technique is downgraded. backend/cache.py keys() returns list(self._store.keys()) with no expiry filtering; expiry is applied lazily in get() only. A key whose feed is never read again lingers for the life of the container. Tonight's /api/debug still listed NVD keys with pubEndDate=2026-09-26 and 2026-09-30 and four www.cisa.gov link-verification paths proxied by the 09-26 run, all days outside any TTL. A present key therefore proves a 200 at SOME time since the backend container started, never a 200 within the last 15 minutes. Do not use it as a freshness or render verdict. Use it only as a lower bound (host allowlisted and reachable at least once) or to spot a feed with NO key at all. Live proof needs one /api/feed fetch per feed, paced per api-rate-limit-on-feed; the 2026-10-04 run did exactly that for all 16 and all answered 200. ### 2026-10-07: this technique carried the ENTIRE of Step 3 tonight, with no browser and no per-feed probing, proving all 12 live feed targets 200 from a single /api/debug call. It is now the primary browserless substitute for the render check. Caveat recorded tonight: /api/debug also retains feedproxy keys from PAST nightly runs' own link-verification fetches (e.g. www.cisa.gov/scuba, a discarded 09-26 guess). Those are probe leftovers, not page feeds, and must not be mistaken for new proxy targets needing allowlist review. ### 2026-10-08: NOT relied on as the primary Step 3 evidence tonight, because the gate was fully open and all 16 feeds were probed individually instead. Recording the preference so it does not drift: live per-feed /api/feed probing with fresh nonces is STRICTLY better evidence and is what a working night should spend its requests on. The cache-key sweep is the fallback for a partially blocked night, and 16 paced probes in batches of four drew no rate limiting. ### RETIRED 2026-10-11, DO NOT USE. The core claim is false. backend/cache.py Cache.keys() returns list(self._store.keys()) with no expiry filter, and eviction happens only lazily inside get(), so an EXPIRED feedproxy key stays listed in /api/debug indefinitely until something requests that exact key. Proven from tonight's data rather than inferred: /api/debug at 04:22Z still listed NVD keys with pubEndDate 2026-10-10T04:36:18 and 04:44:59, the 10-10 run's own timestamps about 24h old, while tonight's genuine load produced a separate 2026-10-11T04:24:06 key. A feedproxy key therefore proves only that the feed returned 200 at some point since the container last started. Establish CURRENT feed health by exercising the feed (browser load, or a nonce'd /api/feed fetch), never from the key listing. Keep one corollary: a key surviving from a previous night proves the backend container has not restarted since, which is a free deploy signal.

frontend/public/sw.js carries a bumped CACHE_NAME constant ('dxedge-v56' as of commit 95afedc) and is served verbatim rather than through the hashed /assets/ bundle. Sharpens webfetch-response-cache-crosses-nights with a worse failure mode: WebFetch can return the body of a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT URL. Tonight the cyber page's production NVD query through /api/feed (a very long URL: /api/feed?url= plus a percent-encoded NVD URL carrying two doubly-encoded ISO timestamps) first failed with CLIENT_ERROR, then on retry with a different nonce returned the HACKADAY radio-hacks RSS feed, and returned Hackaday AGAIN when the nonce was moved to the FRONT of the query string to change the URL prefix. The Hackaday feed had been fetched minutes earlier through the same /api/feed path. So for long /api/feed URLs, neither a fresh nonce value nor a changed prefix reliably separates cache entries, and a plausible-looking feed body is NOT evidence that the feed you asked for is healthy. DIAGNOSTIC THAT WORKED: a SHORT control URL on the same host (/api/feed?url= NVD cveId=CVE-2025-21298) returned correct NVD JSON, proving host, allowlist and proxy were all fine. DEFINITIVE FIX: render the page in the Chromium rig and read the real network log, which showed the exact production NVD query returning 200 with 34336 bytes. RULE for future runs: when a /api/feed probe returns content that does not match the feed requested, do not record either a pass or a fail from it. known_issues_do_not_re_report.detail: A run that wants a full clone after an accidental shallow one must NOT try to delete and re-clone the working directory. rm -rf on the session's own working directory is refused by a built-in safety check that no unattended run can approve, and the refusal is correct rather than an obstacle to route around. Use git fetch --unshallow on the existing clone, then confirm with git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository returning false. Worked 2026-10-20. Cheaper than a re-clone anyway.

A METHOD LIMIT worth knowing before the next feed failure. backend/feedproxy.py maps every upstream non-200 to a 502 carrying the text 'upstream returned <status>', and a timeout to a 504 carrying 'upstream feed timed out'. Those messages are exactly what distinguishes a moved feed (404) from a down feed (503) from a slow one (504). But WebFetch returns error_type SERVER_ERROR with a generic 'There was an error while fetching' and does NOT surface the response body for any 5xx, so a browserless run CANNOT read the precise upstream status. Do not burn calls retrying in the hope of seeing it. What IS available and was sufficient tonight: source=target in the WebFetch error proves dxedge.net answered rather than the egress proxy; a second feed on the SAME host succeeding through the SAME proxy isolates the failure to the path; and the absence of that URL's feedproxy cache key in /api/debug proves no 200 was served, since failures are never cached. That triad is the browserless substitute for reading the status, and it does not require curl or any other substitution.

Security-relevant, pre-existing, and not previously tracked. frontend/src/components/Support.jsx renders the donation QR codes as pointing at a third party: https://api.qrserver.com/v1/create-qr-code/?size=NxN&data=&bgcolor=0e0e0e&color=7affb2&qzone=2. The values passed in the data param are the page's BTC address (bc1q99...dgxl), ETH address (0x450Af...82db), https://paypal.me/sagejw and now https://ko-fi.com/oldtimeradio. CONCRETE RISK, and it is worse than the ordinary third-party-asset case: the QR is the artifact a visitor actually scans, and a compromised, hijacked or MITM'd api.qrserver.com could return a QR encoding a DIFFERENT wallet address while the plain-text address printed next to it stays correct. People scan QR codes without reading the address underneath, so donations would silently redirect with no visible tell and no integrity check available - an cannot carry subresource integrity, and the URL is built fresh on every render. Secondary issues: the addresses are disclosed to a third party on every page view (minor, they are public by design), and the QRs break if the service goes down. PROVENANCE, stated precisely so this is not misread as a regression: Support.jsx was added by James himself in 59111ba on 2026-05-31, and the 7 OTR commits of 2026-10-01 only changed its KOFI constant. The dependency is James's own and about four months old. It surfaced tonight only because reviewing those commits meant reading the file, and it appears in neither known_issues nor awaiting_james, so it has never been reported. NOT fixed autonomously: it is not link rot, not a redirect, not a deprecated feed endpoint and not an /api/feed bypass (an image load is not a CORS fetch and cannot go through a proxy that returns text, same reasoning as otr-audio-is-a-media-element-not-a-feed), so it falls outside all four repair categories. It is also closely analogous to crane-cab-third-party-cdn, which was escalated rather than fixed. OPTIONS: (a) leave as is; (b) generate the QR codes client-side from a vendored QR library, which removes the third party entirely and is the clean fix; (c) pre-generate the four QR PNGs once, eyeball-verify each decodes to the right address, and commit them as static assets, which also removes the runtime dependency and is the smallest change; (d) drop the QR codes and show copy-to-clipboard text addresses only. Recommend (c) for the crypto addresses specifically, since those are the ones where a swap costs real money and the address set almost never changes. The 502 is generated LOCALLY: backend/feedproxy.py MAX_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 = 4,194,304, and fetch_feed raises FeedProxyError('upstream response too large', 502) as soon as the chunked read crosses it. The feed is 1.41x the cap, over by 1,713,935 bytes. Recommended: raise MAX_BYTES in backend/feedproxy.py to 12MB (3x headroom over 5.9MB, and sized with KEV's growth in mind, not just today's number). Consider also streaming to a bounded buffer or capping per-host, since today every request buffers the whole body in memory and the result is cached for the 900s TTL, so the cap is a memory-safety control and not just a nuisance. NOT CHANGED AUTONOMOUSLY: outside the brief's four repair categories and a resource limit on an SSRF-sensitive proxy.
